objective: By the end of this lesson you can work out who must use or be provided with supplemental oxygen on a given flight and for how long, pick and operate the right type of oxygen system, check it before flight, brief your passengers on it, and handle the fire and pressure hazards that come with it.
why: Hypoxia steals judgment first and hides its own symptoms, so the oxygen equipment and your plan for it have to be right before you climb [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Oxygen also makes nearly fireproof materials burn, so the same bottle that protects you can start a fire if it is handled carelessly [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.211

prereading.label: AIM 8-1-2

prereading.label: AC 61-107B 2-7

warmup: Think first: you hold a commercial certificate and a friend asks you to fly him and two coworkers over the mountains at 15,500 ft in his turbocharged single. He owns a portable oxygen bottle with cannulas. Who must breathe that oxygen, who only has to have it available, and how would you know, in flight, that it is really reaching each person?

key_terms.def: Oxygen that meets or exceeds SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard. It is the only oxygen that should be used in aircraft systems [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
A system that flows oxygen all the time, usually for passengers. The mask has a reservoir bag that stores oxygen while you exhale [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
A system that gives oxygen only when you inhale through a sealed mask, mixing in cabin air by altitude. Safe up to 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
Like diluter-demand, but it pushes oxygen into the mask under pressure above 34,000 ft cabin altitude, which makes it safe above 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
A portable electrical unit that senses each breath and gives a pulse of oxygen at the start of inhalation [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
Plastic tubing that runs under the nose to deliver oxygen. More comfortable than a mask but less reliable at higher altitudes [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
A mask that covers only the mouth and nose. Most oxygen masks are this type [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
A fingertip device that shows blood oxygen saturation and heart rate, within one percent of a direct blood measurement [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
The most time a pilot has to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
A loss of cabin pressure in which the lungs decompress faster than the cabin [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. It cuts your time of useful consciousness by at least 50 percent [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A medical device that separates oxygen from the other gases in cabin air and gives the concentrated oxygen to the user [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].
The altitude the air pressure inside the cabin matches. The 91.211 oxygen rule is written in cabin pressure altitude, not airplane altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

chunks.title: Supplemental oxygen at the commercial level

body.p: The Private ACS has no supplemental oxygen Task. It mentions oxygen only as an airplane system you might be asked about (ACS PA.I.G.K1l) and as an example of a system that can malfunction (ACS PA.IX.C.K4). The Commercial ACS gives oxygen its own Task, with knowledge, risk and skill elements, and the examiner can hand you a scenario and ask you to work out how much oxygen it needs (ACS CA.VIII.A.S1).

You already met hypoxia in the Human Factors lesson and the 91.211 table in the Systems lesson. This lesson is about the hardware and the habits: which system fits which altitude, how to check it, how to use it, how to brief people on it, and how to keep it from becoming a fire or a bomb.

bullets: Most high-altitude airplanes have a fixed oxygen installation. If yours does not, portable equipment must be readily accessible in flight [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].
A portable set is usually a container, a regulator, a mask outlet and a pressure gauge [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

Aircraft oxygen is usually stored at 1,800 to 2,200 psi [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. AC 61-107B gives one sizing example: a typical 22 cubic ft portable container holds about 1.5 hours of oxygen for four people at 18,000 ft MSL [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
An oxygen system is a mask or cannula plus a regulator that sets the flow by cabin altitude [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

callout.text: If an oxygen system is installed in an airplane, the design rules say it must protect each user from the effects of hypoxia and be free from hazards in itself, in how it is operated, and in its effect on other parts of the airplane [[60:111|14 CFR 23.2320]]. Your AFM/POH or its supplement tells you how your system works.

check.q: What does the Commercial ACS ask about oxygen that the Private ACS does not?
check.a: A whole Task: rules, physiology, system types, the kinds of oxygen, the hazards, and skills such as working out the oxygen a scenario needs and briefing passengers (ACS CA.VIII.A). The Private ACS mentions oxygen only as an airplane system and a possible malfunction (ACS PA.I.G.K1l, PA.IX.C.K4).

body.p: The Systems lesson put 91.211 in a table. Here, read the words, because each one changes your plan.

head: Words in the rule
What they mean for your plan
rows: Cabin pressure altitude
The rule follows the altitude inside the cabin. In an unpressurized airplane that is your flight altitude; in a pressurized one it is the cabin altimeter [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Required minimum flight crew
In a single-pilot airplane that is you. A passenger in the right seat is not crew [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft
Crew must be provided with and use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes lasting more than 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Above 14,000 ft
Crew must be provided with and use oxygen the entire flight time at those altitudes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Above 15,000 ft, each occupant is provided with
Passengers must have oxygen available. The rule does not say they must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Pressurized, above FL 250
At least a 10-minute supply for each occupant, on top of the paragraph (a) oxygen, for a descent after losing pressure [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Pressurized, above FL 350
One pilot at the controls wears a sealed mask, with an exception up to FL 410 for two pilots with quick-donning masks that go on with one hand within 5 seconds [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]]

body.p: Notice where the minutes come from. Between 12,500 and 14,000 ft the clock gives you 30 minutes before oxygen is required. Above 14,000 ft there is no clock at all. Above 15,000 ft the passengers join the rule [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

callout.text: The legal minimum is not the safe minimum. The AIM and the PHAK both encourage oxygen above 10,000 ft cabin altitude by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Plan the bottle for the altitude you will really fly and the time you will really spend there.

check.q: You fly a pressurized single at FL 230 with the cabin at 9,000 ft. Does 91.211 require anyone to use oxygen?
check.a: No. The rule is based on cabin pressure altitude, and 9,000 ft is below the 12,500 ft trigger. The 10-minute supply rule starts only above FL 250 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

body.p: Your commercial certificate lets you fly for hire, but carrying passengers or property for an operator's customers usually happens under Part 135. Its oxygen rules are stricter. You do not have to memorize them for this Task; know that they exist and that they start lower.

head: Topic
Part 91
Part 135 (unpressurized)
rows: Pilot uses oxygen, lower band
Above 12,500 through 14,000 ft, for the part over 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Above 10,000 through 12,000 ft MSL, for the part over 30 minutes [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]]
Pilot uses oxygen continuously
Passengers
Each occupant provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Oxygen for at least 10 percent of passengers above 10,000 through 15,000 ft for the part over 30 minutes; for each passenger above 15,000 ft [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]
Seeing the supply
Not in 91.211
A way to tell in flight how much oxygen is in each source and whether it is reaching the users [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]
Passenger briefing
Not in 91.211
Normal and emergency use of oxygen if the flight goes above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]

body.p: Part 135 pressurized airplanes have their own lines. Above 25,000 ft each passenger needs at least a 10-minute supply for a descent. Above 15,000 ft each passenger needs a one-hour supply, cut to 30 minutes if the airplane can always descend to 15,000 ft within four minutes [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]].

callout.text: Part 135 moves the pilot rule down 2,500 ft and 2,000 ft: 12,500 becomes 10,000, and 14,000 becomes 12,000 [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

check.q: A Part 135 pressurized airplane is flying with its cabin pressure altitude at 11,000 ft. Which pilot oxygen rule applies?
check.a: The unpressurized airplane rule. Whenever the cabin pressure altitude is above 10,000 ft MSL, each pilot must follow 135.89(a): oxygen above 10,000 through 12,000 ft for the part over 30 minutes, and continuously above 12,000 ft [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]].

chunks.title: Hypoxia up high: impairment, symptoms and useful time

body.p: Altitude hypoxia comes only from lower air pressure. The air is still about 21 percent oxygen all the way up; there is just less pressure pushing it into your blood [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. The Human Factors lesson covered the four kinds of hypoxia. Here the question is how fast it takes away your ability to use your oxygen equipment.

head: Cabin altitude
What the AIM says happens
rows: Night vision starts to suffer [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]

Judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and math get worse; headache, drowsiness, dizziness, euphoria or belligerence. Performance can seriously drop within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]
Above 15,000 ft
Tunnel vision and blue lips and fingernails [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]
Ability to take corrective action lost in 20 to 30 minutes [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]
Lost in 5 to 12 minutes, then unconsciousness soon after [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]

body.p: Impairment is the trap. The first symptoms can be euphoria and a carefree feeling, and hypoxia can leave you sure that everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. A pilot in that state is the least likely person to notice that a cannula slipped off or a flow indicator stopped showing flow.

bullets: Symptoms differ from person to person [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], but they do not vary within one person. That is why the AIM says an altitude chamber flight greatly improves your ability to recognize your own symptoms [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].
Time of useful consciousness drops quickly as altitude rises above 10,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

A rapid decompression shortens it further, because oxygen in the lungs is breathed out fast [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. AC 61-107B puts a number on it: the time of useful consciousness drops by at least 50 percent [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Carbon monoxide, anemia, some medicines, small amounts of alcohol, heat, cold, fever and anxiety all lower the altitude where hypoxia bites [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

head: Altitude
Time of useful consciousness
After a rapid decompression
rows: 20 to 30 min
10 to 15 min
10 min
5 to 6 min
3 to 5 min
1.5 to 2.5 min
1 to 2 min
30 s to 1 min
30 s to 1 min
15 to 30 s

body.p: These are averages from AC 61-107B Figure 2-3, and people vary widely, so the AC says to assume the lower number is the one that limits you [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Fast climbs, physical activity, fatigue, low blood sugar, alcohol, some medicines and smoking all shorten it [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

callout.text: Hypoxia also hurts your eyes. The AFH warns that flying above 10,000 ft by day or 5,000 ft at night without oxygen can impair visual performance [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]. Your scan for traffic and terrain suffers before you feel anything.

check.q: Why does the AIM say altitude chamber training helps, if symptoms vary between pilots?
check.a: Because symptoms do not vary within one pilot. Seeing your own set once in a chamber makes you much better at recognizing it later [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

body.p: The ACS asks for the characteristics, limits and uses of continuous-flow, demand and pressure-demand systems (ACS CA.VIII.A.K3a). The PHAK adds a fourth type you will see a lot in light airplanes: electrical pulse demand.

head: System
How it delivers
Limits and where you see it
rows: Continuous flow
Flows all the time. The passenger mask's reservoir bag stores oxygen while you breathe out, so you get a bigger flow when you breathe in; cabin air is added once the bag is empty [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Usually provided for passengers [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. Certificated up to 41,000 ft MSL, but needs very careful attention above 25,000 ft MSL [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Diluter demand
Only when you inhale through the mask. An automix lever mixes cabin air and oxygen by altitude, or gives 100 percent [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Tight-sealing mask; safe up to 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Pressure demand
Like diluter demand, plus oxygen pushed into the mask under pressure above 34,000 ft cabin altitude, which pressurizes the lungs [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Safe above 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Pulse demand (electrical, portable)
Senses the start of each breath and gives oxygen only in the first part of inhalation, so none is wasted [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]
Can cut oxygen use by 50 to 85 percent compared to continuous flow; most adjust for altitude with a built-in barometer [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]

body.p: Regulators mix by altitude. Most regulators approved up to 40,000 ft give zero percent cylinder oxygen and 100 percent cabin air at cabin altitudes of 8,000 ft or less, changing to 100 percent oxygen at about 34,000 ft. Most regulators approved to 45,000 ft give 40 percent oxygen and 60 percent cabin air at lower altitudes, changing to 100 percent higher up [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].
Some pressure-demand masks carry the regulator on the mask itself. That removes the long hose that must be purged of air before 100 percent oxygen reaches your face [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

callout.text: At high altitude, select the 100 percent setting on a demand or pressure-demand regulator; the PHAK recommends it for crewmembers [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. If you feel symptoms while on oxygen, the AIM says to set the regulator to 100 percent right away [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

check.q: Why is a pressure-demand system safe above 40,000 ft when a diluter-demand system is not?
check.a: It pushes oxygen into the mask under positive pressure, which pressurizes the lungs with oxygen. A diluter-demand system only supplies oxygen when you inhale and is safe up to 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

body.p: The most important thing about any mask is that it matches the oxygen system it plugs into. Crew masks are fitted to the face with little leakage and usually have a microphone. Most are oronasal. A passenger mask can be a simple cup-shaped rubber molding with an elastic strap, or held to the face by hand [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

bullets: Cannulas are more comfortable than masks, but may not give an adequate flow as reliably at higher altitudes [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

The PHAK says airplanes with oxygen systems installed and certified above 18,000 ft must have masks instead of cannulas [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. The current Part 23 rule sets no altitude; it only says an installed system must protect each user from hypoxia [[60:111|14 CFR 23.2320]]. So use a mask above 18,000 ft as the PHAK advises, and follow the limits in your AFM or oxygen system supplement.
Many cannulas have a flow meter in the supply line. If yours has a green flow detector, make it part of your regular scan [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

A beard or mustache must be trimmed so it does not break the seal of a demand mask; check the fit on the ground [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. AC 61-107B goes further: pilots who fly at demand-mask altitudes should not have beards or mustaches at all [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
Pilot masks sometimes allow more oxygen flow than passenger masks, so pilots should use the masks meant for them [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
Keep masks clean: mild soap and water, rinse, disinfect, wipe and air dry. Use a swab, not running water, around a built-in microphone [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

body.p: Portable systems are only as legal as the airplane's paperwork allows. Here is one sample, not a general rule: the W&B Handbook shows an excerpt from one airplane model's type certificate data sheet (Figure 2-15). For that model, flight with a portable oxygen system is limited to 17,500 ft MSL, oxygen must be provided as the operating rules require, and only portable systems listed in its AFM are allowed [[22:29|W&B 2-9]]. Your airplane may have different limits or none, so check your own AFM/POH, supplements and TCDS before you strap a bottle in the back seat.

check.q: You will fly at 16,500 ft with a cannula. What in-flight check does the PHAK suggest?
check.a: If the cannula line has a green flow detector, check it as part of your regular scan [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

chunks.title: Aviator's breathing oxygen and the cylinder

body.p: Not all oxygen is the same. Aircraft containers should be filled with oxygen that meets or exceeds SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and AC 61-107B says only that oxygen should be used [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. When you buy a fill, ask what standard it meets and check the paperwork or labels; a bottle from a shop that fills for other uses is not proof of aviator's breathing oxygen (application).

bullets: High-pressure containers should be marked with their psi tolerance (for example 1,800 psi) before they are filled to that pressure [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

Periodic inspection and servicing keep the system safe [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. A certified maintenance provider must inspect the aircraft system, and a DOT-approved facility must hydrostatic test the oxygen bottles, before use [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

Medical oxygen carried by Part 135 passengers must be of an approved type or meet the hazardous materials marking and labeling rules, be free of flammable contaminants outside, have its valves and gauges protected, and be secured. A compressed-gas cylinder must not be above its rated pressure, and the PIC must be told it is on board and when it will be used [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].
A portable oxygen concentrator is a different machine: it makes oxygen from cabin air instead of carrying it in a tank [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

body.p: Pressure follows temperature. If the volume stays the same, the pressure in a cylinder falls when the cylinder gets colder. So a lower gauge reading after a cold night, or in an unheated part of the airplane, may be the temperature and not a loss of oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. AC 61-107B says the same: a drop in indicated pressure is not necessarily a leak [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

callout.text: Never fill a cylinder above the pressure it is rated and marked for [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]]. A container at 1,800 to 2,200 psi is stored energy [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Fasten it securely before flight [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]], because in an explosive decompression an unsecured oxygen cylinder becomes flying debris [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

check.q: The oxygen gauge read 1,800 psi in a warm hangar last night. This morning, on a cold ramp, it reads less. Did you lose oxygen?
check.a: Not necessarily. Cylinder pressure drops when the temperature drops, so the lower reading may be only the cold [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Still confirm you have enough for the planned flight.

chunks.title: Pulse oximeters: measure, do not guess

body.p: A pulse oximeter clips on a fingertip, shines a special light through it, and reads the color of the red blood cells, which changes as they fill with oxygen. It shows oxygen saturation within one percent of a direct blood measurement, plus heart rate [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

bullets: It is portable and fast, so it is very useful in unpressurized airplanes above 12,500 ft [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
It lets crew and passengers judge their actual need for supplemental oxygen [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
Because hypoxia can make you feel fine [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], the number on the screen is a useful second witness.

But do not rely on it alone. The FAA cautions that waiting for the saturation number to fall can let you become impaired first, and that a fingertip reading may not show how much oxygen your brain is really getting [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

callout.text: Application: read the oximeter at set times, such as level-off and each hourly 5P check [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]], and check passengers too. Neither the PHAK nor AC 61-107B gives a target saturation number, so get one from your CFI, an AME or the oximeter maker before you rely on it.

check.q: How does a pulse oximeter work out your oxygen saturation?
check.a: It sends a special light beam through a fingertip and reads the color of the red cells, which changes as they become saturated with oxygen [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

chunks.title: Preflight and in-flight use of the system

body.p: Before each flight, inspect and test all the oxygen equipment: the available supply, an operational check, and that the oxygen is readily accessible [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Do it with clean hands [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

head: Check
What you are looking for
rows: Mask and tubing
Tears, cracks or deterioration [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Regulator
Valve and lever condition and positions [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Quantity
Enough oxygen for the plan, allowing for a cold-soaked reading [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Gauges, flow indicators, connections
Where they are and that they work [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Don and test
Put the mask on and test the system [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
After any use
All components and valves shut off [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

body.p: The AFH's sample high-altitude training outline lists the same idea as a functional test: supply and pressure, regulator operation, oxygen flow, mask fit, and talking to the pilot and ATC through the mask microphone [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]. If your mask has a microphone, test it on the ground; you do not want to learn it is dead after a decompression.

In flight, put the oxygen on before you reach the altitude where you need it, not after symptoms start. Scan the flow indicator and the oximeter like any other gauge, and check the remaining quantity at each 5P decision point: preflight, before takeoff, hourly or at the midpoint, before descent [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]] [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

callout.text: Smoking during any kind of oxygen equipment use is prohibited [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Say it in the passenger briefing, not after you smell smoke.

check.q: Name four things the PHAK preflight of the oxygen system includes.
check.a: Any four of: clean hands; mask and tubing for tears, cracks or deterioration; regulator valve and lever condition and position; oxygen quantity; gauges, flow indicators and connections; donning and testing the mask [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

body.p: Oxygen does not burn by itself, but it makes other things burn hard. Materials that are nearly fireproof in normal air may burn in oxygen. Oils and greases may ignite if exposed to oxygen, so they cannot be used to seal oxygen valves and fittings [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Oxygen under pressure reacts 'spontaneously' with petroleum products [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

head: Servicing precaution
Why
rows: Read the aircraft service manual first
It names the equipment and the procedure for your system [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]
Service only outside the hangar
Keeps a fire or leak away from enclosed spaces [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]
Wash dirt, oil and grease, including lip salve and hair oil, off your hands; keep clothes and tools clean
Petroleum products and pressurized oxygen react [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]] [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]
Two people for permanently installed tanks
One at the service equipment valves, one watching the airplane's pressure gauges [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]
Not during fueling or other work that could cause a spark
Removes the ignition source [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]
Not with passengers on board
Keeps people away if something goes wrong [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]

body.p: If a fire breaks out at high altitude, AC 61-107B says to start an immediate descent to an altitude that does not require oxygen, and follow the AFM procedures [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]]. Oxygen flowing in the cabin feeds a fire.

Part 135 adds a hard distance for medical oxygen: no smoking or open flame within 10 feet of the oxygen equipment, and only a person trained in medical oxygen may connect or disconnect bottles while a passenger is on board [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].

callout.text: Clean, outside, two people, no fuel truck, no passengers, no smoking. Six things that keep oxygen servicing from becoming a fire [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]] [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

check.q: A mechanic reaches for petroleum thread compound to stop a leak at an oxygen fitting. What do you say?
check.a: Stop. Oils and greases may ignite when exposed to oxygen and cannot be used to seal oxygen valves and fittings [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Use the procedure and materials in the aircraft service manual [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

chunks.title: High-altitude risk and the way down

body.p: A pressurized single can cruise in the 20s with the cabin far lower, but the cabin is only as good as the system. A decompression faster than the lungs can let air out (under about half a second) is explosive; one where the lungs decompress faster than the cabin is rapid [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. Expect noise, a dazed moment, and fog, dust or debris in the cabin [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. A small cabin can lose its pressure 10 to 200 times faster than a large one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. A slow decompression is as dangerous or more so, because it may go unnoticed while hypoxia dulls your mind [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

bullets: Hypoxia is the main danger, so quick and correct use of the oxygen equipment comes first [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. AC 61-107B's hypoxia drill: mask on in 5 seconds or less, check for flow, breathe 100 percent oxygen; descend, preferably below 10,000 ft; land as soon as possible where medical help is available [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Then descend fast. A rapid descent is needed to limit hypoxia, decompression sickness, wind blast and cold [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

If you have no supplemental oxygen, start an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. In a piston airplane, a fast descent from high altitude can cold-shock the engine, but reaching a safe altitude comes first [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

For intense smoke in a pressurized cabin, the AFH says you may need to depressurize at altitude, if oxygen is available for all occupants, or make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Either way, the oxygen has to be there for everyone.

body.p: Fly the emergency descent the manufacturer's way. Where it is not prohibited: power to idle, propeller to low pitch (high rpm), gear and flaps as recommended, and a 30 to 45 degree bank to keep positive G, while staying under VNE, VLE, VFE and, in turbulence, VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Start the recovery high enough to level off safely [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

callout.text: Plan the oxygen for the way down, not just the cruise. Part 91 requires a 10-minute supply per occupant above FL 250 in a pressurized airplane [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Part 135 links the passenger supply above 15,000 ft to whether the airplane can always get down to 15,000 ft within four minutes [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]].

body.p: Application: over high terrain, the lowest safe altitude may still be above 12,500 or even 15,000 ft. Know before takeoff where you can descend to on each part of the route, and carry enough oxygen to get there and stay there.

check.q: What is the first thing you do after a rapid decompression at FL 250, and why?
check.a: Get your oxygen mask on and working, in 5 seconds or less, and breathe 100 percent oxygen. Hypoxia is the main danger, and a rapid decompression cuts your useful time by at least half [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Then start the emergency descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: The examiner will give you a scenario and ask you to brief the passengers on the oxygen equipment (ACS CA.VIII.A.S3). Part 135 requires a briefing on normal and emergency oxygen use when a flight goes above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. The longer Part 91 briefing list that includes oxygen is in Subpart F, which covers large airplanes, turbojet-powered airplanes with more than one engine, and fractional ownership aircraft [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]]. Brief your passengers anyway; the ACS expects it.

bullets: When (application): at what altitude or time you will ask them to start oxygen, and that you may ask them to put it on early.
How: put on the mask or cannula, turn on or plug in the supply, and check the flow indicator or reservoir bag [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
No smoking with oxygen in use [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and no oily hands or hair on the equipment [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
The oximeter: how to use it and to show you the reading [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
Speak up: euphoria, headache, drowsiness, dizziness or tingling may mean hypoxia [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Emergency (application): if you call for it, oxygen goes on first, then seat belts tight for the descent.

body.p: SRM means using every resource you have, inside and outside the airplane [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. For oxygen, that means the oximeter, the flow indicators, ATC, and your passengers' eyes. Ask a passenger to tell you if your cannula slips, and to read their oximeter aloud at each check. With another pilot on board, use CRM, which the AFH pairs with SRM [[24:50|AFH 2-13]]; calling out donning, flow checks and quantity to each other is one way to do it (application).

callout.text: Sustained flight above 5,000 ft, fatigue and late nights can make a pilot less critical and more accepting toward the end of a flight [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]]. Do the hourly 5P check on long flights, and include the oxygen: supply, flow, oximeter, and how you feel [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

check.q: Under which part is an oxygen briefing required when the flight will go above 12,000 ft MSL?
check.a: Part 135: the passenger briefing must cover normal and emergency use of oxygen if the flight goes above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]].

head: Common error
Fix
rows: Using airplane altitude in a pressurized airplane to decide the 91.211 rules
Use cabin pressure altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Thinking passengers above 15,000 ft must wear oxygen
Part 91 says provided with; the crew is who must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Planning to the legal minimum
Plan to the AIM recommendation: above 10,000 ft by day, 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]
Trusting a cannula at any altitude
Use a mask above 18,000 ft as the PHAK advises, and follow the AFM or supplement limits for your system [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Calling a cold-soaked gauge a leak, or a leak a cold soak
Know the cold effect, and still confirm the quantity covers the plan [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Waiting for symptoms before putting oxygen on
Hypoxia hides itself; don it before the altitude, and use an oximeter as a check, not a trigger [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Lip balm, hand cream or oily rags near the system
Clean hands and no petroleum products near oxygen [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Topping up oxygen during fueling or with passengers aboard
Service outside the hangar, not during fueling, passengers off [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]] [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]
Leaving valves on after the flight
Verify all components and valves are shut off after use [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

body.p: There are no numeric tolerances in this Task. The examiner watches whether you apply the right rule to the scenario, run the equipment correctly, give a complete briefing, and use your resources (ACS CA.VIII.A.S1 to S4).

check.q: During your briefing a passenger asks if she has to wear the cannula at 15,500 ft under Part 91. What is the correct answer?
check.a: The rule only requires that each occupant be provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft; the required crew are the ones who must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. You should still encourage her to use it, since the AIM recommends oxygen above 10,000 ft by day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

scenario.title: FL 250 with the owner and two guests
scenario.setup: A business owner hires you as a commercial pilot to fly his pressurized single-engine turboprop under Part 91, with him and two guests aboard, from a sea-level airport to a meeting 2 hours away. You plan FL 250 with the cabin at about 9,000 ft. The airplane has crew masks with a diluter-demand regulator and continuous-flow passenger masks with reservoir bags. The cylinder sat overnight in a cold, unheated hangar.

questions.q: At FL 250 with a 9,000 ft cabin, does 91.211 require any oxygen use or extra supply?
questions.a: No oxygen use, because the rule follows cabin pressure altitude and 9,000 ft is below 12,500 ft. The 10-minute supply for each occupant applies only above FL 250, so at exactly FL 250 it does not [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

questions.q: In cruise a pressurization controller fault lets the cabin climb to 15,500 ft and hold there. What does 91.211 now require of you and of the passengers?
questions.a: You, the required crew, must use oxygen the entire time above 14,000 ft, and each occupant must be provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Put your mask on, give the passengers their masks, and descend so the cabin comes down; the AIM recommends oxygen above 10,000 ft by day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: On preflight the cylinder pressure is lower than the logbook fill. What do you think, and what do you do?
questions.a: A cold soak lowers cylinder pressure without any oxygen being used [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Still confirm the quantity covers the plan, inspect mask and tubing, regulator, gauges and connections, then don your mask and test it [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

questions.q: What do you tell the passengers about their masks before takeoff?
questions.a: Where the masks are, how to put them on, that the reservoir bag stores oxygen while they breathe out [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]], no smoking while oxygen is in use [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and that in an emergency they put their own mask on first. Part 135 would require this briefing above 12,000 ft [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]; under Part 91 it is good practice.

questions.q: Suppose instead there is a bang at FL 250, the cabin fogs and the cabin altitude climbs fast. Why can you not spend time diagnosing first?
questions.a: AC 61-107B gives 3 to 5 minutes of useful consciousness at 25,000 ft, and only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes after a rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Mask on in 5 seconds or less, 100 percent, then emergency descent [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: During the descent, how do you use your resources?
questions.a: Fly the airplane first, then tell ATC you are descending and check each passenger's mask and bag, using everything inside and outside the airplane [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. Level off where the terrain allows, preferably below 10,000 ft, and land as soon as possible [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

skills.do: For the evaluator's scenario, say who must use oxygen, who must only be provided with it, from what altitude and for how long, and show the supply covers it. There is no numeric tolerance; the examiner listens for the right rule applied to cabin pressure altitude.
skills.practice: Work three profiles on paper: Part 91 at 13,500 ft, at 15,500 ft, and pressurized above FL 250; then redo one under Part 135 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]] [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]] [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]. Turn minutes into supply with your system's duration chart.

skills.do: Preflight, turn on, don, check flow and shut off the installed or portable oxygen system, or simulate it if none is installed.
skills.practice: Run the PHAK preflight out loud with the real equipment: mask and tubing, regulator, quantity, gauges and flow indicators, don and test, valves off after use [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Include a mask microphone check if you have one [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].

skills.do: Give a clear oxygen briefing for the evaluator's scenario: when, how to put it on, how to tell it is flowing, no smoking, and what to do in an emergency.
skills.practice: Brief a friend who has never seen the equipment, then have them put it on with no help. Cover the flow indicator or reservoir bag and the no-smoking rule [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

skills.do: Use SRM, or CRM with another pilot: the oximeter, flow checks, quantity checks at the 5P points, ATC and passengers.
skills.practice: On a cross-country, call out a 5P check hourly including supply, flow and oximeter readings, and ask a passenger to watch your cannula [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]] [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

quiz.q: Part 91, unpressurized, cruise at 15,500 ft with two passengers. What does 91.211 require for the passengers?
options: They must use oxygen the whole time
Oxygen only after 30 minutes
Nothing until 18,000 ft
They must be provided with oxygen
quiz.why: Above 15,000 ft cabin pressure altitude each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen; the use requirement is on the required flight crew [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

quiz.q: What does 14 CFR 135.157 require the oxygen equipment to let pilots see in flight?
options: The cabin pressure altitude and the rate at which the cabin altitude is climbing
Each passenger's blood oxygen
The time since the last cylinder fill and the date of the last hydrostatic test
The amount of oxygen in each source and whether it is delivered
quiz.why: The equipment must have a means to determine in flight the amount of oxygen in each source and whether it is being delivered [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]].

quiz.q: Altitude hypoxia happens because, at altitude...
options: The air contains a lower percentage of oxygen than it does at sea level
Carbon dioxide builds up in the cabin faster than the body can clear it
The air pressure is lower, though oxygen stays about 21 percent
The blood loses its ability to carry oxygen as the aircraft climbs
quiz.why: Hypoxia from altitude is due only to reduced barometric pressure; oxygen stays about 21 percent of the air [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

quiz.q: Most regulators approved to 40,000 ft give what mix at a cabin altitude of 8,000 ft or less?
options: Zero percent cylinder oxygen, 100 percent cabin air
40 percent cylinder oxygen and 60 percent cabin air at that altitude
100 percent cylinder oxygen with no cabin air mixed in
50 percent cylinder oxygen and 50 percent cabin air
quiz.why: They give zero percent cylinder oxygen and 100 percent cabin air at 8,000 ft or less, changing to 100 percent oxygen at about 34,000 ft. The 40/60 mix is for most regulators approved to 45,000 ft [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

quiz.q: What does a mask-mounted pressure-demand regulator avoid?
options: The need for a separate microphone built into the oxygen mask
Using oxygen at all above 40,000 ft, where regulators cannot work
The need for a tight seal between the mask and the face
A long hose that must be purged before 100 percent oxygen arrives
quiz.why: Mounting the regulator on the mask eliminates the long hose that has to be purged of air before 100 percent oxygen flows into the mask [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

quiz.q: Per the PHAK, why does a continuous-flow passenger mask have a reservoir bag?
options: To warm the oxygen before it is breathed, so cold gas does not irritate the throat and lungs at altitude
To show the pilot the user is breathing by moving with each breath
To collect oxygen during exhalation, giving higher flow and less dilution on inhale
To store a 10-minute emergency supply for use if the main bottle fails
quiz.why: The bag collects oxygen during exhalation, allowing a higher flow during inhalation with less air dilution; exhaled air goes to the cabin [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

quiz.q: A pilot with a full beard will fly with a diluter-demand mask. What does the PHAK say?
options: Beards do not matter with a demand mask because the regulator adds pressure
Trim it so it cannot break the seal, and check the fit on the ground
Use a cannula instead of the mask at every altitude, so a seal is not needed
Set the regulator to 100 percent oxygen to make up for any leaks
quiz.why: A beard or mustache should be trimmed so it does not interfere with sealing, and the fit checked on the ground [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

quiz.q: Aircraft oxygen containers should be filled with oxygen meeting which standard?
options: USP medical grade oxygen, as sold for hospital and home medical use
SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard
Industrial grade oxygen with a moisture filter fitted at the cylinder
Any oxygen from a sealed cylinder that has no visible damage
quiz.why: The PHAK says containers should be supplied with oxygen meeting or exceeding SAE AS8010 (as revised), the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

quiz.q: How accurate does the PHAK say a pulse oximeter's saturation reading is?
options: Within one percent of directly measured blood oxygen
Within five percent of directly measured blood oxygen
Within ten percent of directly measured blood oxygen
It only shows heart rate
quiz.why: It can calculate saturation within one percent of directly measured blood oxygen, and it also shows heart rate [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

quiz.q: Where should oxygen servicing of an aircraft take place?
options: Inside a clean hangar
Anywhere, if the airplane is grounded
At the fuel pit
Only outside the hangars
quiz.why: Oxygen system servicing should be done only when the aircraft is outside the hangars [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

final_quiz.q: Part 91, unpressurized. You cruise 25 minutes at 13,000 ft, climb and spend 15 minutes at 14,500 ft, then descend to 11,500 ft. When must you use oxygen?
options: The whole flight above 12,500 ft
Only during the 15 minutes above 14,000 ft
Only after the first 30 minutes above 12,500 ft
Not at all, since no single leg lasted 30 minutes
final_quiz.why: Above 14,000 ft the crew uses oxygen the entire time at those altitudes. The 12,500 to 14,000 ft band requires it only for the part over 30 minutes, and you spent about 25 minutes there [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a Part 135 charter in an unpressurized single and climb to 12,500 ft for 20 minutes to top a cloud layer. What applies to you?
options: No oxygen; it is less than 30 minutes
Oxygen only above 14,000 ft
Oxygen continuously while above 12,000 ft MSL
Oxygen only if a passenger asks
final_quiz.why: Under Part 135 each pilot of an unpressurized aircraft uses oxygen continuously above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]].

final_quiz.q: On a Part 135 flight a passenger brings her own medical oxygen bottle. Which is required?
options: The bottle may be filled above its rated pressure for long flights
She may connect and disconnect bottles in flight as she likes
Smoking is allowed if it is more than 3 feet away
The PIC must be told it is on board and when it will be used
final_quiz.why: The PIC must be advised when the equipment is on board and when it is intended to be used; there is no smoking within 10 feet, only a trained person connects bottles with passengers aboard, and pressure must not exceed the rated cylinder pressure [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].

final_quiz.q: You plan IFR at FL 190 in an airplane whose installed oxygen system is certified above 18,000 ft. A passenger wants a cannula because it is more comfortable. What does the PHAK say?
options: Such airplanes must have masks installed instead of cannulas
Cannulas are fine at any altitude as long as the flow is set high
Use a cannula with the regulator set to 100 percent oxygen at FL 190
Cannulas are only limited above 25,000 ft, not at FL 190
final_quiz.why: The PHAK says current regulations require aircraft with oxygen systems installed and certified above 18,000 ft to have masks instead of cannulas, and cannulas may not give adequate flow as reliably at higher altitudes [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

final_quiz.q: How does a typical pulse-demand unit keep up as you climb?
options: An internal barometer raises the oxygen per pulse as altitude increases
You turn up the flow knob by one setting for every 2,000 ft of climb
It switches to continuous flow automatically above 10,000 ft of altitude
It cannot; it is limited to use below 12,500 ft cabin altitude
final_quiz.why: Most pulse-demand systems have an internal barometer that increases the oxygen delivered per pulse as altitude increases [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

final_quiz.q: Why does a rapid decompression shorten the time you have to act?
options: The cabin fills with carbon monoxide that the failed pressurization system pulls in
The oxygen mask stops working when the cabin pressure drops suddenly
Oxygen in the lungs is exhaled rapidly, lowering oxygen pressure in the blood
Cold air slows the heart and cuts blood flow to the brain
final_quiz.why: Oxygen in the lungs is exhaled rapidly, which lowers the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood and reduces effective performance time [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

final_quiz.q: A mechanic wants to stop a small leak at an oxygen fitting with ordinary thread grease. What is the best response?
options: Fine, if he wipes off the excess grease before the system is pressurized again
No. Oils and greases may ignite in oxygen and cannot seal oxygen fittings
Fine, if the system is fully depressurized and the cylinder valve is closed
No, because grease can block the flow through the small fitting passages
final_quiz.why: Oils and greases may ignite if exposed to oxygen and cannot be used for sealing the valves and fittings of oxygen equipment [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: Cruising at FL 240, you notice the cabin altitude has crept from 8,000 to 13,000 ft over the last 20 minutes with no noise and no warning yet. How does AC 61-107B rate this kind of decompression?
options: Harmless, since only rapid or explosive decompressions are dangerous to people
Dangerous only if the cabin fogs or the pressurization warning light comes on
Less dangerous, because a slow decompression gives time to notice and react
As dangerous as or more dangerous than a rapid one, since it may go unnoticed
final_quiz.why: AC 61-107B warns that a slow decompression is as dangerous as or more dangerous than a rapid or explosive one: a rapid one commands attention, while a slow one may go unnoticed and its hypoxia unrecognized [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Get on oxygen and start down now.

final_quiz.q: You fly a night charter at 8,500 ft after a long day. What do the AIM and PHAK recommend about oxygen?
options: Nothing; the regulatory rules start at 12,500 ft, so none is needed at 8,500 ft
Use it only if symptoms appear
Use supplemental oxygen above 5,000 ft at night for best protection
Use it only above 10,000 ft, whether flying by day or by night
final_quiz.why: For optimum protection, oxygen is encouraged above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. The PHAK adds that at night, especially when fatigued, effects may start as low as 5,000 ft [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say to bank about 30 to 45 degrees when starting an emergency descent?
options: To cool the engine by increasing the airflow through the cowling
To slow the airplane down by using the bank as an air brake
To keep positive load factors on the airplane
To keep the cabin pressurized by holding a steady turn rate
final_quiz.why: A bank of about 30 to 45 degrees maintains positive load factors (G forces) at the start of the descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: A Part 135 pressurized airplane cruises above 15,000 ft. It can always descend to 15,000 ft within four minutes. What passenger oxygen supply is required?
options: A 30-minute supply for each passenger
None
A one-hour supply for each passenger
A two-hour supply for each passenger
final_quiz.why: Above 15,000 ft each passenger needs one hour, unless the aircraft can always descend to 15,000 ft within four minutes, in which case 30 minutes is required [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]].

final_quiz.q: Which Part 135 passenger briefing item depends on altitude?
options: Oxygen use, normal and emergency, if flying above 12,000 ft MSL
Location of survival equipment and how the emergency exits operate
Seat belt and shoulder harness use during takeoff and landing
Location of fire extinguishers and how they are used in flight
final_quiz.why: The briefing must cover the normal and emergency use of oxygen if the flight involves operations above 12,000 ft MSL; the other items are briefed on every flight [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]].

final_quiz.q: Late in a 4-hour flight at 11,500 ft, you notice you are agreeing with every plan without thinking. What does the PHAK suggest is going on, and what helps?
options: Normal fatigue; nothing to do until landing
Sustained flight above 5,000 ft and fatigue can make you less critical; hourly 5P checks help you catch it
Carbon monoxide; turn on the heater
Hyperventilation; breathe faster
final_quiz.why: Fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 ft can make pilots less critical and more accepting; on flights over 2 hours, do the 5P check hourly [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]]. Oxygen and an oximeter check fit right into that check [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

takeaways: 91.211 runs on cabin pressure altitude: crew after 30 minutes above 12,500 ft, crew always above 14,000 ft, everyone provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft.
Part 135 is stricter: pilots start at 10,000 ft and use it continuously above 12,000 ft.
Continuous flow for passengers, diluter demand to 40,000 ft, pressure demand above that, pulse demand to save 50 to 85 percent.
Cannulas are comfortable but less reliable up high; the PHAK calls for masks above 18,000 ft, and your AFM or supplement sets the limits for your system.
Fill with aviator's breathing oxygen (SAE AS8010); a cold cylinder reads lower without losing oxygen.
Oxygen plus oil, grease or a flame is a fire: clean hands, no smoking, service outside, never during fueling.
Put oxygen on before you need it. Use the oximeter and flow indicator as checks, but never wait for the oximeter to fall before acting.
cfi_notes: The PHAK TUC table (Figure 17-1) lists '30 minutes or more' at 20,000 ft, but the AIM says the ability to take corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM numbers.

PHAK 7-37 says every occupant above 15,000 ft 'must have' supplemental oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. The rule's words are 'provided with' [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Teach the rule wording: passengers must have it available, not use it.

PHAK 7-38 says 'current regulations' require masks instead of cannulas on airplanes with oxygen systems certified above 18,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. The current Part 23 text in our CFR copy is performance-based and states no altitude [[60:111|14 CFR 23.2320]], and AC 61-107B does not mention cannulas at all [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. The 18,000 ft line rests on the PHAK alone. Teach it as PHAK guidance, plus the limits in the AFM or supplement for the actual system.

The ACS asks for the differences between, and identification of, aviator's breathing oxygen and other types (K3b). The PHAK and AC 61-107B give only the SAE AS8010 purity standard and say only that oxygen should be used [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]; Part 135 adds medical oxygen rules and 14 CFR 1.1 defines a POC [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]] [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. Neither source explains how medical or welding oxygen differs. The common teaching about moisture content is not in these sources, so label it as outside knowledge if you use it.

This AFH edition has no high-altitude operations chapter. Its high-altitude material is the turboprop training outline (AFH 15-14 to 15-15) and the emergency descent [[24:308|AFH 15-14]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

Bring the real equipment to the ground lesson. Have the student don the mask or cannula, find the flow indicator and read an oximeter, then give you a passenger briefing out loud. That covers S2 and S3 in ten minutes.

The PHAK and AIM seem to disagree about symptoms: the PHAK says they vary with the individual, the AIM says they do not vary in an individual [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Both are true: they differ between people but stay the same for one person. Use this to push chamber training.

The PHAK says a rapid decompression reduces effective performance time 'by one-third to one-fourth its normal time', which is hard to read [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. AC 61-107B says plainly that it decreases TUC by at least 50 percent and gives a table [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Teach the AC 61-107B numbers.

The PHAK says the continuous-flow reservoir bag collects oxygen while you breathe out and that exhaled air goes to the cabin [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. AC 61-107B calls it a rebreather bag that lets you reuse part of the exhaled oxygen [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Both agree the bag holds oxygen for the next breath; the lesson's questions use the PHAK wording.
gaps: Apart from one AC 61-107B example (a 22 cubic ft bottle lasts about 1.5 hours for four people at 18,000 ft) [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]], the sources give no flow rates or duration charts. Turning required minutes into 'enough oxygen' needs the system maker's or the AFM supplement's duration chart, plus extra for emergencies [[11:15|AC 61-107B 2-6a]].
Neither the PHAK nor AC 61-107B gives a target oxygen saturation number for a pulse oximeter. Get one from an AME, your CFI or the device maker.

Hydrostatic test and inspection intervals are not given; AC 61-107B says only that a DOT-approved facility must hydrostatic test the bottles before use [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. See the aircraft service manual and the cylinder markings.
How to physically identify aviator's breathing oxygen (cylinder markings, supplier certificates) is not described in the PHAK or AC 61-107B beyond the SAE AS8010 standard.
Exact donning, regulator settings and emergency descent speeds for your airplane come from the AFM/POH, which the AFH says comes first [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

activities.title: Match the rule to what it requires
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then what it requires.

pairs.r: Each occupant provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft cabin altitude
A 10-minute supply per occupant above FL 250, pressurized
Each pilot uses oxygen continuously above 12,000 ft MSL
Oxygen for at least 10 percent of passengers above 10,000 through 15,000 ft, after 30 minutes
A way to see in flight how much oxygen is left and whether it is flowing
Brief passengers on oxygen if the flight goes above 12,000 ft MSL

activities.title: Which oxygen system is it?
activities.intro: Tap a description, then the system it describes.

items.t: A reservoir bag stores oxygen while you breathe out
An automix lever mixes cabin air and oxygen by altitude
Gives oxygen only on inhale; safe up to 40,000 ft
Pushes oxygen into the mask under pressure above 34,000 ft cabin
Pressurizes the lungs, so it is safe above 40,000 ft
An electrical unit senses the start of each breath
Uses 50 to 85 percent less oxygen than continuous flow

activities.title: Parts of a portable pulse-demand system
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: Portable equipment is usually a container, a regulator, a mask outlet and a pressure gauge [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; the pulse-demand unit senses each breath [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. Photo from [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

activities.title: Oxygen through a flight, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Planning: work out who needs oxygen, from what altitude and for how long, and check the supply covers it
Preflight with clean hands: mask and tubing, regulator, quantity, gauges and flow indicators
Don the mask or cannula and test the system on the ground
Turn oxygen on before reaching the altitude where it is needed
In cruise: scan flow indicators and oximeters; check quantity at each hourly 5P check
After use: verify all components and valves are shut off
activities.why: Preflight items and shutoff from [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]; briefing before takeoff from [[6:35|14 CFR 135.117]]; 5P decision points from [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]] and [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

activities.title: True or false: fire and servicing
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Materials that barely burn in normal air can burn readily in oxygen.
cards.why: True. Materials nearly fireproof in ordinary air may be susceptible to combustion in oxygen [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

cards.s: Oxygen servicing is best done inside the hangar, out of the wind and dirt.
cards.why: False. Servicing should be done only with the aircraft outside the hangars [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

cards.s: Permanently installed oxygen tanks usually take two people to service.
cards.why: True. One person at the service equipment valves, one watching the aircraft pressure gauges [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

cards.s: Topping up oxygen while the fuel truck is fueling is fine if the airplane is grounded.
cards.why: False. Servicing is not recommended during fueling or other work that could provide an ignition source [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

cards.s: Service people should wash off lip salve and hair oil before working on oxygen equipment.
cards.why: True. Dirt, oil and grease, including lip salves and hair oil, must be washed off the hands [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

cards.s: Under Part 135, no one may smoke within 10 feet of passenger medical oxygen equipment.
cards.why: True. No smoking or open flame within 10 feet of the oxygen storage and dispensing equipment [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].

cards.s: Servicing oxygen with passengers seated aboard is recommended so the flight is not delayed.
cards.why: False. Servicing while passengers are on board is not recommended [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].

cards.s: AC 61-107B says that if a fire breaks out at high altitude you should descend at once to an altitude that does not require oxygen.
cards.why: True. Because oxygen is so combustible, start an immediate descent to an altitude that does not require oxygen and follow the AFM [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]].

activities.title: Work the oxygen numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Part 135, unpressurized. You fly 80 minutes at 11,000 ft and never go higher. For how many minutes must you use oxygen?
items.why: Above 10,000 through 12,000 ft MSL, oxygen for the part over 30 minutes: 80 - 30 = 50 minutes [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]].

items.q: Part 135, unpressurized, 9 passengers, 50 minutes at 13,500 ft. For at least how many passengers must oxygen be carried?
items.why: Above 10,000 through 15,000 ft, oxygen for at least 10 percent of the passengers for the part over 30 minutes: 10 percent of 9 = 0.9, so at least 1 passenger [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]].

items.q: A cylinder reads 1,800 psi at 70 F. Overnight it cools to -5 F with no oxygen used. About what will it read? (Pressure varies with absolute temperature: F + 460.)
items.why: Pressure varies directly with temperature at constant volume [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Application with absolute temperatures: 70 + 460 = 530 R; -5 + 460 = 455 R. 1,800 x 455 / 530 = 1,545 psi, a drop of about 14 percent with no oxygen lost.

items.q: A bottle lasts 2.5 hours for one person on continuous flow. A pulse-demand unit cuts oxygen use by at least 50 percent. At least how many hours should the same bottle last with it?
items.why: Pulse demand reduces the oxygen needed by 50 to 85 percent [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]. Using half the oxygen doubles the time: 2.5 / (1 - 0.50) = 5.0 hours (application).

items.q: Part 135, pressurized. To carry only a 30-minute passenger supply above 15,000 ft, the airplane must always be able to get down to 15,000 ft within four minutes. From FL 250, what average descent rate is that?
items.why: The 30-minute supply is allowed if the aircraft can descend to 15,000 ft within four minutes [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]. 25,000 - 15,000 = 10,000 ft; 10,000 / 4 = 2,500 fpm.

activities.title: Over the mountains on a cannula, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You fly a turbocharged, unpressurized single under Part 91 with three friends across a mountain range at 15,500 ft, about 2 hours. You have a portable oxygen bottle with a pulse-demand unit, cannulas for everyone and one mask.

steps.s: The day before, a passenger offers a spare oxygen bottle from his welding shop so you will have extra.
options: Take it; oxygen is oxygen, and extra supply only adds a safety margin on a long flight
Take it and mix it into your bottle once the pressures look about the same
Take it but use it only for passengers and keep your own bottle for yourself
Decline unless it is aviator's breathing oxygen and fits your approved equipment
steps.why: Only oxygen that meets or exceeds SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard, should be used [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Also check your AFM: in one sample TCDS, that airplane allows only portable systems listed in its AFM [[22:29|W&B 2-9]].

steps.s: At preflight you grew a full beard on vacation and plan to use the one mask yourself.
options: Fly; the mask will seal fine because a full beard only fills in small gaps
Check the fit on the ground and trim the beard if it breaks the seal
Turn the regulator up to a richer setting to make up for leaks
Skip oxygen and stay at 12,500 ft without telling anyone
steps.why: A beard or mustache must be trimmed so it does not interfere with the mask seal, and the fit checked on the ground [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

steps.s: Climbing through 13,000 ft, one passenger's line shows no flow on its flow indicator. She says she feels great.
options: Check her cannula and connection, get flow back or switch her to another outlet, and watch her oximeter
She feels fine, so ignore it
Climb faster to get above it
Turn off all oxygen to save it
steps.why: A flow detector check belongs in your scan [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. Hypoxia can feel like everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and an oximeter shows her real need [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]. Above 15,000 ft she must be provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

steps.s: Level at 15,500 ft, a passenger reaches for a cigarette lighter.
options: Allow it if he takes his cannula off first
Stop him: no smoking while oxygen equipment is in use
Allow it if the window vent is open
Allow it below 10,000 ft only
steps.why: Smoking during any kind of oxygen equipment use is prohibited [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

steps.s: Halfway, your 5P check shows the bottle will run out about 15 minutes before you clear the high terrain.
options: Continue and hope the wind improves
Use less oxygen yourself and save it for passengers
Change the plan now: reroute or divert to land where you can descend, before the supply runs out
Climb higher for a tailwind
steps.why: The midpoint 5P check is there to catch problems while good options still exist [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]]. Above 14,000 ft you must use oxygen the entire time [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], and hypoxia steals judgment first [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].
